learning_objective: 🎯 Organize large amounts of data into rectangular arrays and learn the special rules to add, multiply, and transform them like a computer!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A matrix is simply a rectangular grid of numbers or functions arranged in rows (horizontal) and columns (vertical). It is the backbone of computer graphics and programming!
The order tells you the size of the matrix. It is written as 'm x n' (read as 'm by n'), where 'm' is the number of rows and 'n' is the number of columns.
Multiplying matrices isn't just multiplying the matching spots. You have to multiply the ROWS of the first matrix by the COLUMNS of the second matrix. It's a specific pattern!
Taking the transpose is like flipping the matrix over its diagonal. All the rows become columns, and all the columns become rows.

fun_activity.title: 🏪 The Shop Inventory Grid
fun_activity.instructions: Create a 2x3 matrix representing the number of pens, pencils, and erasers sold in two different shops. Now, create another matrix for the price of each item, and try multiplying them to find the total revenue!

exam_tips: 📌 Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative! $AB$ does not always equal $BA$. Always keep the order exact.
📌 To check if two matrices can be multiplied, ensure the number of columns in the first matrix equals the number of rows in the second.
📌 Remember the rule for transpose properties: $(AB)' = B'A'$. Notice how the order reverses!
quick_recap: ⭐ Matrices are ordered rectangular grids of numbers.
⭐ You add matrices element-by-element, but you multiply them row-by-column.
⭐ A matrix is symmetric if it is exactly the same as its transpose ($A = A'$).
